full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is plaintiff's appeal by leave against the judgment dated August 16, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 255 of 2000 making absolute the Rule upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated October 28, 1999 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Gazipur in House Rent Appeal No.1 of 1998 dismissing the same and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated April 30, 1998 of the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Sadar, Gazipur in House Rent Case No.1 of 1997 decreeing the same. 

 3. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff' let out the premises in suit i.e. shop Nos. 1 and 2, to the defendant by an agreement dated September 1, 1988, that initially rent was fixed at Taka 2.50 per square foot but later on the rent was enhanced to Taka 3.00 per square foot but the defendant did not, pay the rent at enhanced rate, that three sons of the plaintiff are graduates but could not procure any employment and, as such, to provide these unemployed sons plaintiff requires the shop in question. It was also the case of the plaintiff that defendant without obtaining permission from him made construction on the southern side of the shop No.1 and also installed illegal electric connection in the shop, that the defendant caused disturbance to the other tenants of the market, that notices under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act were served on October 19, 1996 and December 2, 1996 terminating the tenancy but the defendant did not vacate the premises in suit, Hence the suit. 

 4. The suit was contested by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the defendant is not a monthly electable tenant as per the agreement, that he purchased the possessory right of the shop at a consideration of Taka 95,000 and running medicine business there, that in spite of payment of rent regularly the plaintiff did not grant receipt and thereupon he filed the House Rent Case No.1 of 1993 and depositing the rent in, the said case, that the house rent case was allowed by the trial Court and, as against that, plaintiff did not file any appeal, that plaintiff's case of default by the defendant in the payment of rent is not true and that she has some other shops in the market to meet her alleged requirement. Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. The defendant moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The said Division made the Rule absolute on the findings that the plaintiff received Taka 95,000 as 'salami' and thereupon, handed over possession of the premises in suit, that in the agreement by which the defendant was put into possession there is no clause to terminate the tenancy or to eject the tenant, that as the plaintiff has other shops in the market "requirement as made out by the landlord do not appear to be bonafide. Facts of the case also do not disclose that the landlord was pressingly in need of the suit shops. Moreover, under the terms of the agreement, on such requirement the tenancy could not be brought to an end. Secondly, the view of the appellate Court that when the possessory right was transferred that does not; debar the landlord from getting a decree for ejectment is wholly misconceived in the facts and circumstances of the case. It may be noted that the landlord is entitled to possession only in tenus of the agreement of lease as executed by him/her and not otherwise. After handing over the possession of the premises at a valid consideration the landlord voluntarily forfeits her right of possession on such flimsy ground of requirement". Thereupon, the Division set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 9. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the High Court Division was in error in holding that as possession of the premises in suit was made over to the defendant on receiving Taka 95,000 as advance, and there being nothing in the agreement of tenancy about termination of the tenancy on the ground of bona fide requirement, the plaintiff or, in other words, the landlord was not entitled to terminate the tenancy since by letting out the premises in suit on taking advance the landlord did neither transfer his title nor put an embargo on the statutory right of terminating tenancy in case of bonafide requirement. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel that the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that as the landlord received Taka 95,000 as premium for handing over possession of the premises in suit to the defendant and, as such, because of the said manner of handing over possession of the premises in suit, the plaintiff forfeited her right of taking possession upon ejectment of the tenant. In support of the aforesaid contention the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Mustaque Hossain vs Md Shajahan Miah and another reported in 57 DLR (AD) 60. In the reported case section 10 of the "বাড়ী ভাড়া নিয়ন্ত্রন আইন, ১৯৯১” (Act No.3 of 1991) (the Ain) came up for consideration. Section 10 of the Ain reads as: 

 10. The fact of the aforementioned case was that the landlord, since required the premises in suit for the purpose of giving accommodation to his son to start business and thereupon terminated the tenancy. The tenant having had not vacated the premises, the landlord filed the suit. The suit was resisted by the tenant contending, amongst others, that he purchased the possession of the premises in suit on payment of Taka 3,00,000 and two lease deeds were executed between the landlord and the tenant fixing rent Taka 200 for each of the shop rooms. In the agreement between the landlord and the tenant, there was a clause whereby the tenant was given right to sell the possession of the suit shops to a 3rd party. It was the definite case of the tenant that he purchased the possession of the suit shop rooms on payment of Taka 3,00,000. 

 11. The provision of section 10 of the Ain prohibits the practice of receiving any premium, salami, security or any amount similar or akin to the same for letting out any premises and renewal of the tenancy or for extension of the tenancy. The provision of the said section also prohibits receiving of any amount exceeding rent of one month without permission of the House Rent Controller. So, it is seen that the provision of section 10 of the Ain prohibits the practice of handing over possession of the premises by the landlord receiving amount exceeding rent of one month with the stipulation of allowing the tenant to transfer his tenancy right or possession of the premises in suit to a 3rd party. In the background of the provision of law as in section 10 of the Ain, in the reported case, it has been observed: "Section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 makes the illegal practice of payment of salami prohibited and that the tenant is entitled to refund of the salami paid by him within 6 months of such payment under section 14 and the landlord was liable to pay fine for receiving salami under section 3 of the said Act. The widespread and long standing practice of voluntary payment of salami in the commercial world did not make the tenant a nonejectable one and no interest other than the tenancy right recognised by law could be created on payment of salami so as to prevent the tenant not liable to be ejected on specific legal ground for the purpose. Under section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act, the landlord is entitled to eject a tenant as soon as a monthly tenant is a defaulter or a landlord bonafide requires the premises or for building and rebuilding purpose. 

 13. In the background of the law as in section 10 of the Ain and the decision of this Court in the reported case, we are of the view the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgment of the lower appellate Court affirming the judgment of the trial Court on the view that as the landlord had handed over possession of the premises in suit upon receiving an amount more than one month's rent as advance, landlord forfeited his right of asking the tenant to hand over possession on the ground of bonafide requirement or seeking redress under the law in case of refusal by the tenant to hand over possession on the ground of bonafide requirement of the landlord. 

 14. The trial Court, on consideration of the materials on record, held that the landlord requires the premises in suit for bonafide requirement and the said finding and decision of the trial Court was affirmed by the appellate Court. The High Court Division has not made any finding negating the finding and decision of the courts below as regard the case of the plaintiff that she requires the premises in suit for her bonafide requirement i.e. for making provision for her unemployed sons by starting business, but has observed that plaintiff is not entitled to get back the possession of the premises in suit on the flimsy ground of bonafide requirement since she upon receiving good amount of money as advance handed over possession of the premises in suit and thereby she voluntarily forfeited her right of possession of the premises in suit. 

 15. The law is now settled that a tenant who obtained possession of a premises upon making advance of an amount which is more than rent of one month of the premises in suit and in the agreement of the tenancy there is stipulation that the possession so obtained upon making advance would be transferable to a third party which the landlord would accept or the tenancy would be nonejectable, the stipulation so made in the agreement of tenancy being violative of the provision of section 10 of the Ain and also being void in view of the provision of section 23 of the Contract Act, the tenant would be an ejectable tenant on the ground of anyone of the grounds as are in section 18 of the Ain. Since in the instant case plaintiff proved her requirement of the premises in suit for her use and occupation and, as such, the defendant in the background of the discussions, made hereinabove was required to surrender the premises in suit and having had not done so voluntarily the plaintiff approached the Court for obtaining possession of the premises in suit for her bonafide use and occupation and, as such, the Court of first instance and the appellate Court in the background of the facts of the case were not in error in decreeing the suit. 

 18. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that while reversing the judgment and decree of the Courts below the submission of the respondent that plaintiff has other shops in the market and as such, plaintiff's case of bonafide requirement of the premises in suit is not entertain able weighed with the said Division. 

 19. In the case of Abdus Salam Bepari vs Shamsun Nahar Bibi and others reported in 6 BLC (AD) 36, the question of ejectment of a tenant from a particular shop in a particular market on the ground of bonafide requirement while the landlord has some other shops in the same market or in the same building came up for consideration and it has been held that it is the landlord's choice to eject a tenant from a particular premises on the ground of bonafide requirement and that when the landlord's case of bona fide requirement is established then the relief sought for ejectment of a particular tenant from a particular premises would not be refused only because in the same locality or in the same building the landlord has other shops which have been let out and instead of proceeding against the others the landlord was proceeding against the shop in suit, but that would not disentitle the landlord to have the decree of ejectment sought in respect of the premises in suit. The aforesaid question also came up for consideration before this Court in the case of Zaher Ahmed vs Manik Sardar reported in 6 MLR (AD) 44 and therein it has been held- 

 20. Fact of the aforesaid case is that landlord instituted the SCC suit for eviction of the defendant from a shop room on the ground of his bonafide requirement. The prayer for ejectment was opposed by the tenant that he obtained the possession of the premises in suit upon making advance of Taka 55,000 and an agreement for lease was executed between him and the landlord fixing rent of the premises in suit at Taka 240 per month and the said rent was subsequently enhanced to Taka 375. The trial Court decreed the suit. As against that the tenant moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not arrive at the finding that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the tenant and that trial Court also did not arrive at the finding that there was a compelling necessity on the part of the landlord for bonafide use of the premises and that the landlord malafide picked up the tenant to evict with the intention to let out the premises in suit to others at enhanced salami where he had more shop rooms.
